title: Tracking Body Composition in Healthy Aging
abstract:
### Aging, Body Composition, and Fall Risk  
[Aging is associated with body composition changes](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0167494322000929), such as decreases in skeletal muscle mass and increases in fat, especially in visceral and abdominal fat accumulation. [Chua et al (2021)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12877-021-02226-6) found that “In oldest-old adults, visceral fat area was the best discriminator for obesity associated with mobility disability.” Declines in skeletal muscle mass and muscular function may be associated with increased fall risk. Accurately monitoring these vital changes requires an advanced body composition analyzer. [Chao et al (2025)](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jcsm.13788) conducted a longitudinal study on muscular function and fall risk in older adults, noting “Promoting muscle function should be prioritized as a preventive strategy to mitigate adverse clinical outcomes.” [Suzuki et al (2025)](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-91101-0) tracked fall risk and the usage of diabetes medications in older adults across a median of 2 years, with the authors stating, “The increased risk of falls due to the intake of SGLT2 (sodium glucose cotransporter 2) inhibitors was ascribed to the concomitant decrease in skeletal muscle mass, increase in urinary frequency, and decrease in blood volume.”
## Successful Strategies for Healthy Aging  
[Diet](https://www.geriatric.theclinics.com/article/S0749-0690%2820%2930050-1/abstract), [physical activity](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12603-021-1665-8?fbclid=IwAR3dJkeHjgcSrR9Xq5kBfN-HLrbpli8WcAnz7AeY5Nu9XcGCHEB07Sd2z1w), and other lifestyle factors can have a significant impact on healthy aging. A 24-week resistance training program in older women with obesity by [Kim et al (2022)](https://www.mdpi.com/1660-4601/19/21/14554) observed that the not engaging in resistance training “negatively affected body composition, bone mineral density, functional fitness, and isokinetic muscle strength.” [Martins et al (2024)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405457724001566) organized a 16-week high-speed resistance training program where older adults in the intervention group had “significant improvements in phase angle,” and the authors concluded that resistance training “could effectively prevent the decline in cellular health and cell integrity in older adults.” Phase angle (PhA) is an estimate of cellular health that has been associated with fat free mass (please refer to our [previous blog post on PhA](https://inbodybwa.com/blog/phase-angle-an-indicator-of-cell-membrane-health/)).This measurement can be reliably tracked using an advanced body composition analyzer, like the [InBody S10](https://inbodybwa.com/inbody-s10/).
